# The Custodians

In a glass case in a hallway at the University of Queensland, a funnel full of black pitch has been dripping since 1930. "Dripping" is generous. Since the physicist Thomas Parnell cut the funnel's sealed stem and let the pitch begin its descent, nine drops have fallen. The most recent came in 2014. Pitch at room temperature feels solid. Strike it with a hammer and it shatters like glass. But given enough time, it flows. Parnell wanted to show his students that the categories we use for matter, solid and liquid, are really statements about patience. Something that seems solid to you might be a liquid to a sufficiently unhurried observer.

For more than fifty years the experiment's custodian was a physicist named John Mainstone. He took over in 1961 and looked after the funnel until his death in 2013. He never saw a drop fall. He came close several times. In 1979 a drop fell over a weekend when he wasn't there. In 1988, the story goes, he stepped away for a few minutes to get a drink and missed it. In 2000 the university had set up a webcam to catch the event, and the camera failed during the crucial window. Mainstone died the year before the ninth drop fell.

The story is usually told as a gentle comedy of bad luck, and it is that. But I keep returning to a different aspect of it. Mainstone spent half a century tending something whose defining events he could not reliably witness. The experiment did not need him to watch it. It needed him to keep it: to make sure nobody moved the case, nobody threw it out during a renovation, nobody decided it was a strange old curiosity taking up hallway space. His job was not observation. It was continuity.

---

There is a small and odd category of human undertakings that are designed, or have come, to outlast the people who start them. I find them moving in a way that is hard to articulate, so I want to try.

In the Clarendon Laboratory at Oxford, there is a bell that has been ringing since 1840. More precisely, two small bells sit beneath a pair of dry piles, an early kind of battery, and a tiny metal clapper swings between them, carrying charge back and forth. It has been doing this for nearly two centuries, an estimated ten billion times or so. You can't really hear it; it sits behind glass, and the sound is too faint. Nobody knows exactly what the piles are made of, because finding out would mean taking the thing apart, and nobody wants to be the person who stopped the Oxford Electric Bell. So it continues, a question that no one will answer because answering it would end it.

In 1879, a botanist named William James Beal buried twenty bottles on the campus of what is now Michigan State University. Each held sand mixed with seeds from a couple of dozen species of plants, mostly weeds. His question was practical: how long can seeds lie dormant in the soil and still grow? Farmers wanted to know how long a field would keep producing weeds after you stopped letting them go to seed. Every so often, one bottle is dug up and the seeds are planted to see what sprouts. At first the interval was five years, and later it was stretched to ten and then twenty, to make the bottles last longer. The most recent dig was in 2021, carried out at night, in secret, by a small group of researchers who hold the map. A few seeds of moth mullein, buried when Rutherford B. Hayes was president, sprouted. The next dig is scheduled for 2040. If the schedule holds, the last bottle will come up around the end of this century.

Beal died in 1924. The people who will dig up the final bottle have almost certainly not been born yet, or are small children now, with no idea that a hand-drawn map of a patch of earth in East Lansing is waiting for them.

And in a half-ruined church in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is playing a piece by John Cage called *Organ²/ASLSP*. The initials stand for "As Slow As Possible." Cage didn't specify how slow, which is the kind of invitation that attracts a certain kind of person. The performance began in 2001 with a rest, a silence of about seventeen months. The first chord sounded in 2003. The notes are sustained by weights on the organ's pedals and keys, and every so often, sometimes years apart, a small crowd gathers to watch a note change. The performance is scheduled to end in 2640. The number was chosen partly because Halberstadt claims one of the earliest documented large church organs, built in 1361, and 2000 minus 1361 is 639. So the piece is meant to last as long as that history, a mirror held up across six centuries.

---

What unites these things is not really science or art. The pitch drop is barely an experiment anymore; everyone knows what it will do. The Oxford bell has long since stopped being a research instrument. The Cage performance is, among other things, a gentle joke. But each has quietly become something else: a test not of pitch, or batteries, or seeds, or music, but of us. Can a group of people, over generations, keep a promise nobody alive made?

The answer, so far, is yes, and I think that's remarkable, because the forces against it are enormous. Institutions reorganize. Buildings get renovated. Funding priorities shift. A new department head arrives who doesn't see the point. Wars happen. The Oxford bell has survived two world wars. Beal's bottles have survived the transformation of a small agricultural college into a university of fifty thousand students, with all the construction that implies. The map has been passed from hand to hand, each custodian choosing their successor.

It would be very easy for any of these to end. That they haven't tells you something about the kind of care human beings are capable of when the object of care is small, specific, and clearly entrusted to them.

---

There's a Japanese shrine complex at Ise that has been rebuilt every twenty years for well over a thousand years, with interruptions. The main sanctuaries are torn down and reconstructed, identically, on adjacent plots. The wood is new each time. The shrine itself, as a physical object, is never more than two decades old. And yet it is also among the oldest continuous things in Japan.

Western ideas of preservation tend to focus on the original material. We want the actual stones, the actual canvas, the actual timber. A restoration that replaces too much feels like a kind of forgery. Ise suggests another view: what is being preserved is not the wood but the knowledge of how to build with it. Twenty years is roughly the span in which a young carpenter can learn from an old one and then, in turn, become the old one. The rebuilding is a mechanism for passing skill forward. If you rebuilt only every hundred years, no one who built the last one would be alive to teach the next.

I think the long experiments work the same way, even though they look like the opposite. The pitch drop is continuous in material. It's the same pitch Parnell heated and poured. But its survival depends entirely on the unbroken chain of people who knew it mattered. The object persists because the story persists. Mainstone inherited not just a funnel but a reason, and he kept the reason alive as much as the pitch.

---

I want to be careful not to get too sentimental about this, because there's a version of the argument that curdles into worship of mere endurance. Lots of things persist for bad reasons: inertia, cowardice, sunk costs, the refusal to admit that something has outlived its purpose. Institutions keep useless rituals. Bureaucracies keep forms nobody reads. Not everything old deserves to continue.

What seems different about the custodial experiments is that they are cheap, harmless, and voluntary. The pitch drop costs almost nothing to maintain. Beal's bottles take up a few square feet of soil. The Halberstadt organ is funded by donations from people who find the idea delightful, including some who pay to sponsor a particular year of the performance and have their names on a plaque. Nobody is being made to carry these things. They are carried because people want to carry them, which is a very different kind of persistence from the grim continuation of a dead policy.

And they do something that I think is genuinely useful, even if it isn't scientific. They train the imagination to operate on a longer timescale than it naturally wants to.

---

Human attention is built for short intervals. We evolved to track the movements of prey, the moods of the people around us, the turn of seasons. A year is a long time to a person. A decade feels like an era. A century is, for most of us, an abstraction. We know intellectually that it is a hundred years long, but we don't feel it.

Many of the most important problems we face, though, unfold on timescales that exceed our intuitions. Climate changes over decades and centuries. Soil forms over millennia and can be lost in a few generations. Forests planted today will be mature long after the planters are gone. Radioactive waste stays dangerous for longer than recorded history. Even something as ordinary as a public library or a well-built bridge is a gift from people who mostly never met the ones who benefited.

I don't think the pitch drop is going to solve any of this. But I think there is value in having, scattered around the world, small concrete objects that make long time visible. A funnel that has produced nine drops in nearly a century. A bottle that holds seeds from 1879. A chord that will hold for years. They are like the scale bars on a map: small, easily overlooked, but necessary for understanding the size of what you're looking at.

---

There's another group of long projects that are less whimsical and perhaps more important: the longitudinal studies. The Framingham Heart Study began in 1948 by enrolling thousands of residents of a small Massachusetts town, and it is now following their grandchildren. Much of what we know about the risk factors for heart disease — blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking — came into focus through it. There's also a Harvard study of adult development that began in 1938 with a cohort of undergraduate men, and later expanded to include a group of boys from inner-city Boston. It has followed them through war, marriage, divorce, illness, and death, and has since moved on to their children. Its most frequently quoted finding is almost embarrassingly simple: the quality of people's close relationships turns out to be one of the strongest predictors of their health and happiness in old age.

What strikes me about these studies is that they can only answer questions that someone decided to ask decades earlier. The researchers in 1938 could not know what the researchers in 2000 would want to learn. They had to guess, to collect data broadly enough that it might be useful to people with different theories, different tools, different concerns. It's an act of faith in the curiosity of strangers.

That faith is the thread running through all of it. When Beal buried his bottles, he was trusting that someone in 2021 would still care about the germination of moth mullein. When Parnell cut the funnel stem, he was trusting that the university would still be there, that the hallway would still be there, that someone would still find it worth keeping. When the organ in Halberstadt began its silence, the people who started it were trusting that in 2640 there would be a church, and a town, and a reason to let the final note end.

---

Sometimes when I think about the future, I feel a kind of vertigo. Not quite despair, but a sense of how much could go wrong, how many threads could be cut. The long experiments are a small corrective to that. They are evidence, modest but real, that people do in fact keep faith with strangers across time. Not always, not perfectly, but more often than you might predict.

It's worth noticing how little heroism is involved. Mainstone was not a hero in any grand sense. He was a physicist who kept an eye on a funnel, gave interviews when journalists came around, and made sure the thing wasn't thrown out. The Beal custodians are botanists who dig a hole every twenty years. The Halberstadt volunteers move weights on an organ. The work is small. The continuity is made of small work, repeated, handed off, accepted.

I suspect that's true of most things that last. We tell stories about founders and visionaries, the people who start things. We tell far fewer about the people who keep them going: the second custodian, the fifth, the eleventh. But it is the keepers, not the founders, who determine whether anything survives. A beginning is a single act. Continuity is ten thousand acts by people who mostly go unnamed.

---

I sometimes imagine the person who will dig up Beal's last bottle. They will probably be a botanist, maybe in the middle of their career, handed a map by someone older. It will be night, because the digs are done at night to keep the location secret. They will dig carefully. They will bring the bottle back to a lab, and plant the seeds in trays, and wait.

Maybe nothing will grow. Two centuries is a long time, even for a seed. Or maybe, in some tray under grow lights, a single pale shoot will push up through the soil: a plant whose parent grew in a Michigan field before the telephone was common, before cars, before anyone flew. And the person who planted it will look at it and feel, I hope, some of what Beal must have hoped someone would feel. Not triumph exactly. Something quieter. A sense of having been part of a very long sentence and getting to write the last word.

And then the experiment will be over. The map will have no more use. The custodians will have no more custody. That's the thing about these projects that I find most beautiful and most strange: they are made to end. The pitch will eventually run out of the funnel. The Cage piece has a final note. Beal's bottles are finite. They are not attempts at eternity. They are attempts at a very long, very specific span of time, with a beginning and an end, entrusted to people who will each hold it only for a while.

That seems to me like a good model for a life, or for most of what we do that matters. You inherit something you didn't start. You keep it for a time. You probably won't see the moment it was all building toward. Mainstone didn't. You hand it on. The drop falls when it falls, whether or not you're watching. What you were responsible for was never the drop. It was keeping the funnel safe, and making sure someone else would care after you were gone.

The ninth drop fell in April 2014. It was caught on camera. Mainstone wasn't there to see it, but the thing he kept was.
